title: What makes a band's or player's style
summary: Section sounds, stock arrangements and the tone, environment and ideals that shape style.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: I thought I'd get off on a long ramping subject. And it came to me. We talked one time about what style it was, you know, like a man could be reading music, say reading lead saxophone part and give an entirely different sound of the section. Absolutely.

But you can see that today in say a band like Les Elgart. It's true that they have distinctive music in the arrangement but there is also a distinctive sound to the sax section as they follow the leader. A very distinctive sound, different from any other band. But there was much more of that in those days. For every band the section would have a distinctive sound. Sometimes in the brass it was harder to do this in the brass but Isham Jones' brass had a distinctive sound to it. And very often the sax because there was so much leeway all the way from a lombardo style to a much more solid style and then the style that Goodman introduced when he had the first Mandela and then Jaime Schertzer playing lead sax. Very distinctive sounds. But earlier, this is what make a band. A lot of bands had nothing but stocks. But they all sound quite different. They cut up stocks a little bit. They make their own cuts and sort of maybe put the ending up for an introduction and things like that to make their band sound a little different. But the main difference came from the fact that the way they play these things. They took quite a lot of liberties. Not just with the sound but sometimes they even took liberties with the actual way the music was written and the side men, the section men, just had to follow the leader. They got used to the way they played. This made it very hard to bring a strange man in the band, you see.
But what do you think it is that makes for a style?
I'm talking about either in section work or solo or what have you.

Well, partly of course, insofar as the style depended on tone, even his mouth formation would have something to do with that and perhaps the way he learned to blow, the kind of strength he had and the tone he produced. But then, a feeling, you get into the intangibles again and that feeling might be in part something innate but also in part the whole environment that he grew up in. The men he listened to, the men he worked with, the thing that soaked into him most to give him his approach. And then of course, the last and ultimate thing, I guess no guy ever really gets quite what he's looking for. He has a kind of ideal and he strives very hard to play that way but most all people fall short of their ideal. I've seen many musicians slam the horn down, throw it against the wall, not just because they missed a note but because generally they weren't getting what they were trying to get as a harp. And they'll mess around with mouthpieces and new horns and everything else. And if they're happy and successful, they're always coming closer to that ideal way of
